newsitem.title: GREECE: ATHLETICS-JOHNSON TO APPEAL AGAINST COURT DECISION.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-JOHNSON TO APPEAL AGAINST COURT DECISION.

text.p: Banned Canadian sprinter Ben Johnson will appeal against a ruling handed down by an Ontario judge last week upholding his life ban from the sport.
Johnson's agent Morris Chrobotek said in a telephone interview from Toronto on Wednesday that he also planned to take the case to the International Amateur Athletic Federation (IAAF) council.
"We intend to appeal against last week's decision which upheld Ben's ban and be back in court in the next two or three weeks," Chrobotek said.

"What I also want to do now is take the case direct to the IAAF council. I want them to give me five minutes of their time and hear us out on why he should be re-instated. I also intend contacting member federations of the IAAF and the Prime Ministers of those countries and tell them exactly how the IAAF is run.
"It sits as both judge and jury on its athletes and that is totally wrong."
Chrobotek also revealed a plan to help athletes who fall foul of the doping rules.

"We are planning to establish an organisation to help athletes in a similar plight to Ben. It is going to be called the International Amateur Athletic Support Federation and will stand up to the hypocrisy that is the IAAF.

"Soon there will be so many athletes facing bans from competing they will need a body to represent them and make sure they get a fair hearing. Everyone knows the IAAF could clean up the sport in 24 hours if it wanted to, but it persists in keeping up a total sham.
"There is also another point here that has never been addressed.

"During 1987 and 1988 Athletics Canada were clearly aware of what was happening and that certain athletes were using drugs. But Ben ended up with a life ban. What punishment was ever taken against the Canadian federation. The IAAF still works with those people. What sort of a joke is that ?
"It is well known that Ben Johnson was not the only athlete using banned drugs at the time -- but it suited the IAAF to turn a blind eye to most other cases and use Ben as a scapegoat."
Johnson, now 36, became the focus of the century's greatest sporting scandal after winning the Olympic 100 metres title in a world record time of 9.79 seconds at the 1988 Seoul Olympics.

Shortly after the race he tested positive for the anabolic steroid stanozolol, was stripped of his title and his world record was struck from the books. He was also banned for two years but after being re-instated in 1990, was banned for life three years later after high levels of testosterone were found in his system.
Last week Ontario Judge Moira Caswell rejected his application that that life ban consituted an illegal restraint of trade.

Johnson, his manager and lawyers have been galvanised into action partly because time is running out for the sprinter to even consider competing again and also because the IAAF are considering halving its four-year ban for drug offences at its two-day congress which began here today.
The IAAF have been forced by recent court decisions to consider a reduction in the ban, partly because some countries have ruled that a four-year ban effectively constitutes restraint of trade.
